title: Masei: one date of death (Numbers 33:38)
hookLine: the only death the Torah dates exactly is Aaron's

lines: DATES THAT ARRIVE ON THEIR OWN.
THE LIST STOPS FOR A DEATH.
cards: Some dates live in a phone calendar. Others arrive on their own, without a reminder: the week a parent died, the day the house burned, an anniversary nobody else seems to remember.
They come back every year, whether anyone writes them down or not. In the middle of the long list of campsites, the Torah suddenly stops. Between one station and the next, it pauses for a death.
And it does something rare: it gives the exact date.

teach.h: THE FORTIETH YEAR, FIFTH MONTH, FIRST DAY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord's command and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month.
Then: Aaron was a hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on Mount Hor. Year, month, day and age. That is rare.
Even Moses' death, at the end of Deuteronomy, comes without a date.

teach.h: NO DATE FOR MOSES IN THE TORAH.
teach.b: The rabbis later worked out a traditional date for Moses, the seventh of Adar, by calculating from other verses, but the Torah itself doesn't say. For Aaron, it does.
The fifth month in the Torah's counting is the month later called Av, so Aaron died on the first of Av. The Torah had already told the story of his death back in Chukat; here it marks the day. Why?
The text doesn't explain. But Jewish life has kept the instinct.
The anniversary of a death, by the Hebrew calendar, is called a yahrzeit, a Yiddish word meaning a year's time.

On that day the custom is to light a candle that burns for a whole day, say the mourner's Kaddish, give charity, and sometimes study in the person's memory. Some communities mark Aaron's own yahrzeit on the first of Av.
A death is not just an event in the story; it's a day that comes back, and here the Torah marks the day.

how: The yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, is commonly marked by lighting a candle that burns for a full day, saying the mourner's Kaddish, and often giving charity in the person's memory.

games.q: you're writing down a long list of campsites. in the middle, the high priest dies. what do you record?
o: the year, month, day and his age.
games.why: the Torah stops the list to give the fortieth year, the fifth month, the first day, and his age: a hundred and twenty-three.

practice: Think of a date that holds someone: the day a grandparent died, the day a friend was born, the day you got sober, the day a child came home.
If you pray, you might say their name; if not, simply hold them, or that moment, for a few breaths.
